Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Open by naming that some people in any room have lived through this and can step out, and keep every example about the characters. If a student discloses something, don’t promise secrecy; walk them to a counselor that day.

Every student in the room

Survivors of every gender are in the room, and who someone tells first depends on family and culture; say clearly that it is never the victim's fault and that boys and nonbinary students can be hurt too.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Keep it light for ten seconds, then go straight to the next slide.

Slide 2 · Notes

Say it slowly. Nobody will be asked about their own life. If someone steps out, check in after.

Slide 3 · Notes

Ask: what happens if an app just takes your location without asking? (People get mad.) Same with people.

Slide 4 · Notes

Ask: which check do you think gets skipped most? Freely given means no fifth ask, guilt trip or pressure from someone with power.

Slide 5 · Notes

Take a few guesses. The reflex is human: it happens to anyone, of any gender.

Slide 6 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 7 · Notes

Even adults misread each other in a three-minute speed date. Guessing in a dark room goes worse.

Slide 8 · Notes

If a student defends it, answer with the fact, not their character. At least half of college assaults involve alcohol (Abbey, 2002).

Slide 9 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 10 · Notes

Say directly: boys and nonbinary students get hurt too, and often tell no one.

Slide 11 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 12 · Notes

Ask the room which check fails before the next slide.

Slide 13 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 14 · Notes

Capacity fails. Whatever was said doesn’t count if someone can’t follow what’s happening.

Slide 15 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 16 · Notes

Specific and ongoing. A photo sent to one person is never permission to show anyone.

Slide 17 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 18 · Notes

A no needs no reason: “I don’t want to.” “Not tonight.” “Stop.” Then the other person says okay and changes course, no sulking.

Slide 19 · Notes

Two minutes in pairs. It feels awkward, and that’s the point: it gets smoother with practice.

Slide 20 · Notes

Take four or five. Praise the ones that sound like real people.

Slide 21 · Notes

Quiet moves count. Distract and delegate work for students who hate confrontation.

Slide 22 · Notes

Direct, distract or delegate? Take a few, then show one good move.

Slide 23 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 24 · Notes

Don’t ask questions that sound like blame. They decide what happens next.

Slide 25 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 26 · Notes

Don’t present one route as the right one. Consent fits every family value too: it covers every touch and every photo.

Slide 27 · Notes

Two minutes in pairs. Nobody speaks for a group, and no personal stories.

Slide 28 · Notes

Take a few. Listen for strengths as well as costs.

Slide 29 · Notes

Share the student page link. Close with: if something happened, it’s not your fault. Stay in the room a few minutes after.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can run any situation through the four checks (capacity, freely given, specific, ongoing), explain why silence or freezing isn't a yes, and practice asking, taking a no, and stepping in as a bystander. Survivors in the room should hear, clearly, that it wasn't their fault.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 3 minBefore we start, and every app has to ask
  2. 6 minFour checks, all four every time
  3. 5 minFreeze, and no answer is not Allow
  4. 4 minTwo myths, one per slide
  5. 9 minDoes the yes count? Dev and Nina, Jules, Leo
  6. 6 minAsking well: turn and talk, share out
  7. 7 minThree ways to step in: Maya, a friend’s story
  8. 5 minEvery student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Before we start, every app has to ask, the four checks, no answer is not Allow, one does-the-yes-count scene, asking well, and the close.

Before you teach
Assume survivors are in the room.

Say at the start that this topic is personal for some people, anyone can step out, and nobody will be asked about their own life. Keep every example about the characters on the slides.

Say "not your fault" out loud.

Whatever someone drank, wore or said before. Put it on the board. A survivor in the room may never hear it said this plainly anywhere else.

If a student discloses.

Thank them, stay calm, and don't promise to keep it secret. Walk them to a counselor that day. Counselors can explain what they'd have to share and with whom.

Shut down victim blaming gently.

If someone says "well, she was drunk," answer with the fact: responsibility belongs to the person who went ahead without consent. Then move on without shaming the student who said it.

Be accurate about the law.

In Massachusetts, a person under 16 can't legally consent to sex, with no close-in-age exception. Sharing explicit images without consent is a crime as of 2024, including AI fakes. Don't add more than that.

Use anonymous questions.

The best questions in this lesson come on cards. Read them before answering, and skip any that name a real person.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Every gender.

Boys and nonbinary students are assaulted too and are often less likely to tell. Say it directly, and include "guys always want it" in the myths.

LGBTQ+ students.

Use examples with same-gender couples alongside others, and never make consent sound like a rule only for boys pursuing girls. Outing someone, or threatening to, is a form of pressure.

Who they tell first.

Depending on family and culture, a student might first tell a friend, sibling, aunt, coach, faith leader or counselor. Any start counts. Don't present one route as the right one.

Faith and family values.

Some students come from families or faiths where dating or sex before marriage isn't accepted. Consent applies to every kind of touch and every photo, so the lesson fits all of them. Never assume students are sexually active.

Disability.

Students with disabilities face higher risk and are often treated as unable to say yes or no. Capacity means being able to understand and decide, and a disability doesn't take that away.

Fear of police or reporting.

Some students fear what reporting means for their family. Medical care helps even without a report, RAINN is confidential, and the student decides what to do next.

What the research says

70% of 298 women seen after a sexual assault reported significant involuntary paralysis during it, and 48% extreme paralysis (tonic immobility).

Möller, Söndergaard and Helström, Acta Obstetricia et Gynecologica Scandinavica, 2017

In speed dating, men on average overestimated women's sexual interest, and women tended to underestimate men's.

Perilloux, Easton and Buss, Psychological Science, 2012

At least half of sexual assaults among college students involve alcohol, drunk by the person who did it, the person it happened to, or both.

Abbey, Journal of Studies on Alcohol, 2002

In 2021, 14% of U.S. high school girls said they had been forced to have sex at some point, the first increase in ten years.

CDC Youth Risk Behavior Survey, 2023

Across 39 studies of more than 110,000 teens, about 15% had sent a sext, 27% had received one, 12% had forwarded one without permission, and 8% had their own forwarded.

Madigan et al., JAMA Pediatrics, 2018

Across 26 Kentucky high schools, schools that trained students to step in had less sexual violence in the years that followed.

Coker et al., American Journal of Preventive Medicine, 2017

In Massachusetts, a person under 16 can't legally consent to sex. Since 2024, sharing someone's explicit images without consent is a crime, including AI fakes, and most teens are sent to an education program instead of being charged.

Massachusetts General Laws c. 265 § 23; St. 2024, c. 118
